701.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
701.hook: Garuda steals the nectar of the gods to buy his mother's freedom, and never tastes a drop
701.carry: the price paid, to the letter
701.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
701.howItsDone: In some Vishnu temples Garuda stands facing the shrine with folded hands, as Vishnu's mount, and kusha grass is used in some Hindu rites. Some families retell Garuda's story to children as a story of loyalty to a mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kadru's bet, black hairs on a white horse, and a curse on the sons who refused to cheat. The curse fell on the innocent.

An egg cracks open and something blazing comes out, so bright the gods take it for fire. It's Garuda, Vinata's son, a bird of enormous strength. He grows up to find his mother a slave to her sister, made to carry the snakes wherever they want to go. So he asks the snakes the obvious question: what would it take to set her free? They name a price nobody could pay. Bring us the amrita, the nectar of immortality, which the gods keep for themselves.
screen: `A BLAZING EGG.` → `HIS MOTHER, A SLAVE.` → `THE PRICE: THE GODS' NECTAR.`

segments.voice: So Garuda goes to get it. He fights the gods who guard it, slips past a spinning wheel of blades, gets by the fierce guardians beside the nectar, and takes the amrita. The first surprise: he doesn't drink it. He could make himself immortal on the spot, and he carries it away untouched, because it's for his mother's freedom. Vishnu is so pleased that he grants Garuda boons: a place on Vishnu's banner, and immortality without a drop of the nectar. Garuda offers a boon in return, and Vishnu asks him to be his mount. Indra, king of the gods, strikes him with the thunderbolt, and Garuda, the text says, lets a single feather fall out of respect for it, and nothing more. Then Indra asks for the nectar back. Garuda makes him an offer: I've promised it to the snakes, and I'll let no one drink it. But wherever I set it down, you may take it up. They part as friends. The second surprise. Garuda sets the nectar down for the snakes on a bed of kusha grass. Here it is, he says. My mother is free. Go and bathe before you drink. While they bathe, Indra comes down, as agreed, and takes the amrita back to heaven. The snakes return to an empty bed of grass and lick it, hoping for a drop, and the sharp grass splits their tongues. That, the story says, is why snakes have forked tongues, and why kusha grass is held holy: the nectar of the gods once lay on it. Garuda kept every promise to the letter. And the snakes who held his mother as a slave got exactly what they bargained for, and nothing more.

segments.voice: Garuda carried the gods' own nectar and never took a sip. Bring to mind something you're carrying for someone else, an errand, a secret, someone's trust, and feel its weight lightly. Breathe in and hold it carefully; breathe out and notice any pull to keep a little for yourself, without judging it.

702.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
702.hook: a tired king drapes a dead snake on a silent sage, and a chain of small choices ends in Takshaka's bite
702.carry: no single link is the whole story
702.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
702.howItsDone: Vows of silence, mauna, are kept by some Hindu ascetics and by some householders for a day or a season. Parikshit's death is also the setting of the Bhagavata Purana, which tradition says was recited to him in his last days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Garuda, the nectar he never tasted, and his mother set free. The price paid, to the letter.

A king is out hunting, and he's lost a deer he wounded. He comes on an old sage sitting very still, and asks: did a deer pass this way? The sage says nothing. He's keeping a vow of silence. The king asks again. Nothing. And the king, tired, hungry and stung, lifts a dead snake on the end of his bow and drapes it over the old man's shoulders. Then he rides home. The king is Parikshit, Janamejaya's father. The sage is Shamika. This is how Janamejaya's wound was made.
screen: `A LOST DEER, A SILENT SAGE.` → `A DEAD SNAKE ON HIS SHOULDERS.` → `JANAMEJAYA'S WOUND.`

segments.voice: Shamika doesn't move. He bears it. But his son Shringin, a young man with a hot temper and real power from his austerities, hears about it from a friend, and curses the king: within seven nights, Takshaka, king of the snakes, will bite him, and he will die. Now watch the father. Shamika is not pleased. Forgiveness is a sage's strength, he tells his son, and the king protects people like them. He sends a disciple to warn Parikshit. The king takes the warning seriously. He builds a palace on a single pillar and fills it with guards, physicians, and holy men with mantras against poison. A sage named Kashyapa, who can cure snakebite, sets out to save him. Takshaka meets him on the road, bites a great tree to test him and burns it to ash, and Kashyapa brings it back to life. So Takshaka offers him wealth to go home, and Kashyapa takes it and turns back. Then the snakes come disguised as ascetics, carrying fruit for the king. In one fruit is a tiny insect. As the sun goes down on the seventh day, Parikshit, thinking the danger has passed, picks it up and says, half in jest: let this one bite me. The insect becomes Takshaka, coils around the king, and kills him. Look at the chain. A wounded deer. A sage's silence. A king's insult. A son's curse. A healer paid off. A joke at sunset. That's the frame Janamejaya stands in, and his fire is the next link.

703.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
703.hook: a young sage, half from the snakes' own family, asks the king for one gift: stop the fire
703.howItsDone: In some Hindu households Astika's name is remembered as a protection against snakes, in keeping with the promise the story records. A reciter working through the Adi Parva in order finishes the Astika section before turning to the Kuru story proper.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a dead snake on a silent sage, a son's curse, and Takshaka hidden in a fruit. No single link is the whole story.
screen: `NO SINGLE LINK IS THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: The fire is lit. Janamejaya has heard how his father died, and his priests begin the snake sacrifice. As they chant, snakes are drawn from everywhere into the flames, the text says, great and small, crying out as they fall. Takshaka, the one the king most wants, has fled to Indra for protection. And a young man is walking toward the sacrifice, sent by his mother. His name is Astika. His father is a sage, his mother is the sister of a snake king, and he has come to stop the fire.
screen: `THE FIRE IS LIT.` → `TAKSHAKA HIDES WITH INDRA.` → `A YOUNG SAGE IS COMING.`

segments.voice: Astika's story starts with his father, a sage named Jaratkaru, who wanted no wife and no home. One day he found his ancestors hanging head down over a pit, holding on to a thin root that a rat was gnawing. They were falling, they told him, because their line would end with him. So Jaratkaru agreed to marry, on strange terms: only a bride who shared his name. The snake king Vasuki had a sister named Jaratkaru. Vasuki knew his mother Kadru's curse, and he had been told that a child of this marriage would save the snakes. That child is Astika. At the sacrifice, Astika doesn't argue or threaten. He praises the king, the priests and the fire, so well that Janamejaya wants to give him a gift. Ask for anything, the king says. And Astika asks: stop the sacrifice. The king tries to bargain, offering other gifts. Astika says no; this is what I want. By now Indra has let go of Takshaka, and the snake king is falling toward the flames, held in the air above them. The assembly urges the king to keep his word, and Janamejaya does. The fire stops. Takshaka is spared. The text adds that the snakes, in gratitude, promised safety to those who remember Astika's story. And at this same sacrifice, the text says, Vaishampayana told Janamejaya the story of his ancestors, the Kurus and the Pandavas. So the frame closes on a king who let go of his revenge and sat down to hear about his family's great war. On the first day of this year we met him beside a fire. We leave him listening.
screen: `A SAGE WHO WANTED NO WIFE.` · `A BRIDE WHO SHARED HIS NAME.` · `PRAISE, THEN ONE REQUEST.` · `THE KING KEEPS HIS WORD.` · then, large: `WE LEAVE HIM LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Astika stopped a fire not by fighting it, but by asking. Bring to mind something you'd like to see stop, a quarrel, a habit, a cold silence between two people, and notice whether you've been arguing with it. Then let a question form instead: what would I ask for, if someone offered?

704.title: Shantanu and Ganga
704.hook: a king in heaven stares too long at the river goddess, and gods under a curse ask her for a terrible favor
704.carry: where the eyes go, a life follows
704.howItsDone: At the Ganga, the river is honored as a goddess: pilgrims bathe in her waters, some carry Ganga water home in sealed vessels, and lamps are offered to her at evening aarti on her banks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Astika asked, the fire stopped, and Janamejaya sat down to hear the story. We leave him listening.

A court in heaven. The gods are gathered before Brahma, and among them is a king, Mahabhisha, who earned his place there by his deeds on earth. Then the river goddess Ganga arrives. A wind lifts her garment. The gods lower their eyes. Mahabhisha doesn't. He looks, and keeps looking. Brahma sees it, and tells him: you will be born again among mortals. This part of the Kuru story starts with a stare.
screen: `A COURT IN HEAVEN.` → `THE GODS LOWER THEIR EYES.` → `ONE KING KEEPS LOOKING.`

segments.voice: This opens a new story inside the Adi Parva: Shantanu and Ganga. The text sets it up with two curses, side by side. The first is Mahabhisha's. Brahma sends him down to be born on earth, and tells him that Ganga, the one who stole his mind, will cross him there, and that his time on earth will end when he finally loses his temper with her. Mahabhisha chooses to be born as the son of a good king named Pratipa. The second curse belongs to the Vasus, a group of gods. On her way back, Ganga meets them, downcast. The sage Vasishtha, they tell her, has cursed them to be born as men, and they don't want to linger in human lives. So they ask a strange favor: be our mother on earth, and as each of us is born, throw us into your waters, so we're set free at once. Ganga agrees, with one condition: one son has to live, so that her time with the king isn't fruitless. Each Vasu gives a portion of his own power to that son, who will live a long life on earth and, they say, have no children. Hold that detail; it matters for a long time. Now go back to the fault that started it. Not a crime, not a lie: a look that wouldn't lower, in a hall where every other eye looked down. Brahma's sentence is shaped to fit it. The one who took his mind in heaven will try it on earth. Where Mahabhisha's attention went, his whole next life followed. And Ganga here is both the sacred river and a woman with a promise to keep.
screen: `MAHABHISHA: BORN AGAIN ON EARTH.` · `THE VASUS: CURSED BY VASISHTHA.` · `THROW US INTO YOUR WATERS.` · `ONE SON MUST LIVE.` · then, large: `WHERE THE EYES GO, A LIFE FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: A river keeps moving; it doesn't hold on, so let the breath do the same for a few rounds, eyes lowered or closed. 705.title: Shantanu and Ganga
705.hook: a woman rises from the river and sits on a praying king's right thigh; years later his son makes her a promise
705.howItsDone: In some Hindu weddings, the couple's promises to each other are made aloud before a sacred fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahabhisha, a stare in Brahma's court, and the Vasus' strange bargain with Ganga. Where the eyes go, a life follows.
screen: `WHERE THE EYES GO, A LIFE FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: A king is sitting by the river, deep in prayer. His name is Pratipa. Out of the water rises a woman of great beauty, and she sits down on his right thigh. Pratipa doesn't send her away, and he doesn't take her as a lover. Instead he tells her: the right thigh is for children and daughters-in-law. The left is for a wife. You sat on the right, so you'll be my son's wife.
screen: `A WOMAN RISES FROM THE RIVER.` → `SHE SITS ON THE RIGHT THIGH.` → `YOU'LL BE MY SON'S WIFE.`

segments.voice: The woman is Ganga, and she agrees: she'll marry Pratipa's son, on one condition, that whatever she does, he won't question it. Pratipa and his queen long for a son, and a son is born: Shantanu, who is Mahabhisha come down from heaven. When Shantanu is grown, Pratipa hands him the kingdom, and a message with it. A lovely woman may come to you. If she does, take her as your wife. Don't ask who she is, and don't question what she does. Shantanu loves to hunt. One day, walking along the bank of the Ganga, he sees a woman by the water, and he's struck. He asks her to be his wife. She answers with terms. Whatever I do, good or bad, you must never stop me or speak harshly to me. The moment you do, I'll leave. He agrees. Now notice what we know that Shantanu doesn't. We know she's Ganga. We know about the Vasus and her promise. He knows only that he's in love, and that he's given his word. The poem sets a promise in place long before anyone sees what it will cost. A vow made happily, in the first rush of love, becomes the thing that will hold his tongue. And Pratipa prepared the ground. His message reads almost like a warning passed from father to son: when something wonderful comes, don't ask too much. They marry, and the text says they're happy together. And their first child is on the way.

706.hook: seven sons are given to the river while a king keeps his vow of silence; at the eighth, he speaks
706.carry: the riverbank isn't the whole story
706.howItsDone: Many Hindu families carry the ashes of their dead to the Ganga, at places such as Haridwar and Varanasi, trusting the river as Ganga is trusted in this story: as a mother whose waters release.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pratipa, a father's warning, and Shantanu's promise never to stop or question her. A vow made in love.

A son is born to the king and queen. And the queen carries the baby down to the river, and gives him to the Ganga's waters. As she does it, she says it's for his good. Shantanu watches from the bank, and says nothing. He remembers what he promised: never stop her, never speak harshly to her, or she leaves. Another son is born, and the same thing happens. And another. The text tells it plainly, without looking away.

segments.voice: Seven sons, the text says, one after another, into the river. Every time, Shantanu stays silent, afraid that if he speaks, she'll leave him. Then the eighth son is born. As she carries this one toward the river, Shantanu can't hold it in. Don't kill him, he says. Who are you? Why do you kill your own sons? She stops. I won't kill this one, she says. But my time with you is over, as we agreed. And she tells him who she is: Ganga, the daughter of Jahnu, the text says. The sons were the Vasus, cursed to be born as men, and she has freed them as she promised. Two days ago we heard the Vasus ask for this. Yesterday we watched the vow get made. Today we see what it cost, and the scene can be seen three ways. For Shantanu, these were his children, lost in front of him. For the Vasus, it was the release they asked for. For Ganga, it was a promise kept to the letter. The Mahabharata doesn't smooth this over; it lets the scene stay hard. Some readers take it as curses and karma working themselves out. Some hear in it what an unquestioning vow can cost. Some take from it that what's seen from the riverbank isn't the whole story. The son who lives carries the Vasus' power, and their word that he'll have no children. Ganga takes the child with her, and goes.

707.title: Shantanu and Ganga
707.howItsDone: Some Hindu households and temples keep and care for cows and honor them as sacred. Vasishtha's Nandini belongs to the wondrous cows of Hindu story, cows said to give what is wished for.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Vasus, seven sons given to the river, and the eighth spared when the king finally spoke. The riverbank isn't the whole story.

His wife has just told Shantanu she is Ganga, and that his seven lost sons were the Vasus, gods under a curse. His promise is broken, and she's about to go. So he asks the one thing he still can: what did the Vasus do, that they had to be born as men and die as babies? Ganga answers him before she leaves. Her answer starts on a mountainside, with a sage and his cow.
screen: `WHAT DID THEY DO?` → `GANGA ANSWERS BEFORE SHE GOES.` → `A SAGE AND HIS COW.`

segments.voice: The sage is Vasishtha. He keeps his hermitage on a mountain slope, and he owns a wondrous cow named Nandini. One day the Vasus come wandering there with their wives. One of the wives sees the cow and wants her, not for herself, but for a friend on earth, a princess, so that her friend might stay young and free of illness. Her husband is a Vasu named Dyu. He knows whose cow this is. But to please his wife, and with his brothers helping, he takes her. Vasishtha comes back to an empty pasture, sees with a sage's inner sight what happened, and curses the Vasus: they will be born on earth as men. The Vasus come and beg him to take it back. Here's the part to notice. Vasishtha can't unsay the curse. But he can shape what follows it. The seven who helped, he says, will be freed soon after they're born. Dyu, the one who took the cow, will live a long life on earth: virtuous and learned, devoted to his father, and with no children. So the eighth son, the one Shantanu saved by speaking, is Dyu, the thief himself. Then Ganga takes the child and goes. These days have turned on words that bind: a son's curse on a king, a young sage's single request, a sentence in Brahma's court, a vow by a river. And now a sage who can't take back his words, and spends his next ones making them bearable.
